Am Mittwoch, 31. Oktober 2012 11:27:56 UTC+1 schrieb Havard Rue:
> for now, use the 'z' model, not the wrapper-based one.
>
>
>
> On Wed, 2012-10-31 at 11:06 +0100, Håvard Rue wrote:
> > Hi
> >
> > as Ryan suggested, there is a undocumented model called 'z'. this has
> > been around for quite a long time, but its internal implementation is
> > based on a 'hack' (and is hard to maintain) and therefore I want to
> > remove it and replace it with something more appropriate. morover, the
> > 'z' model do
> >
> > linear.predictor = ..... + Z %*% z
> >
> > where z ~ N(0, prec * I), and Z is a fixed matrix, and the prior for
> > (log)prec is hyper=list(prec = list(prior=..,param=...)))
> >
> > the model is internally expanded into 'm' submodels, so you'll get
> > results like this
> >
> > r$summary.random$idx.1$mean
> >
> > for the first element of 'z', and .2 for the second etc.
> >
> >
> > looking at the joint distribution for
> >
> >         (Z %*% z, z)
> >
> > we can rewrite this as a 'generic' model. this is the idea in some new
> > code, which is a wrapper to existing models,
> >
> > new.z.model = inla.model.wrapper(covariates = Z,  model="joint",
> > Q = diag(m))
> >
> > r = inla(y ~ 1 + f(idx,  model=new.z.model),
> >         data = list(y=y, idx=idx))
> >
> >
> > and then you'll get the posterior for (Z %*% z, z), so what you're after
> > is here:
> >
> > r$summary.random$idx[(n+1):(n+m),"mean"]
> >
> >
> > as the last 'm' elements of that vector.  this model is more general as
> > 'z' can have any prior precision matrix. the prior for its scaling, can
> > be set with hyper = list(prec = list(...))) as before
> >
> > it might be we can do the 'wrapper'-call internally in the f-function,
> > so it will be hided from the user
> >
> > to conclude: there is an approach on its way out, and a new better one
> > on its way in, but neither ones are stable. the new one is 'in progress'
> > and needs more work. I'll put this on the todo-list.
> >
> > OOPS: in the future then model 'z' will go away and the new 'wrapper'
> > one will be changed (or even appear as something else, as we're not
> > convinced about the general usefulness of the 'wrapper'-based models),
> > but I'll post it here when its done.
> >
> >
> >
> > *******************
> >
> > EXAMPLE:
> >
> > z = rnorm(m)
> > Z = matrix(rnorm(m*n), n, m)
> > y = 1 + Z %*% z
> > idx = 1:n
> >
> > r = inla(y ~ 1 + f(idx,  model='z',  Z = Z),
> >         data = list(y=y, idx=idx, Z=Z))
> >
> >
> > new.z.model = inla.model.wrapper(covariates = Z,  model="joint", Q =
> > diag(m))
> > r = inla(y ~ 1 + f(idx,  model=new.z.model),
> >         data = list(y=y, idx=idx))
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > new.z.model = inla.model.wrapper(covariates = Z,  model="joint", Q =
> > diag(m))
> > r = inla(y ~ 1 + f(idx,  model=new.z.model),
> >         data = list(y=y, idx=idx))
> >
> > print(r$summary.random$idx[(n+1):(n+m),"mean"] - z)
> >

messages.subject: Deviance and DIC in missing data models
messages.subject_clean: Deviance and DIC in missing data models
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I am using INLA to fit some space-time small area estimate models for poverty rates in the US.  I have lots of missing data, as many areas do not have annual estimates, so i'm trying to use INLA to estimate them. My question is about how INLA calculates Deviance or DIC in missing data models.  I assume that for missing data, no deviance is calculated for the missing element, for example of what I'm doing here are some fake data:

N<-rpois(n=1000, lambda=30000)
Y<-rbinom(n=1000, size=N,prob=.15 )
t<-c(rep(1,100),rep(2,100),rep(3,100),rep(4,100),rep(5,100),rep(6,100),rep(7,100),rep(8,100),rep(9,100),rep(10,100) )
id<-rep(1:100, 10)
test2<-data.frame(Y=Y, N=N, time=t, id=id)

missing<-sample(1:1000, size=100, replace=F)
test2$Y[missing]<-NA
test2$N[missing]<-NA

mod2<-Y~1+f(id, model="iid")+f(time, model="rw1")

fit2<-inla(formula=mod2, Ntrials=N, data=test2, family="binomial",
           control.compute=list(dic=1), control.predictor=list(compute=T, link=1))

summary(fit2)

which gives:
Model hyperparameters:
                   mean      sd        0.025quant 0.5quant  0.975quant
Precision for id   116872.86  36116.54  61522.23  111741.34 202038.93
Precision for time  75770.56  35286.15  26385.42   69601.49 161624.15

Expected number of effective parameters(std dev): 82.17(4.928)
Number of equivalent replicates : 10.95

Deviance Information Criterion: 9931.07
Effective number of parameters: 82.41

Marginal Likelihood:  -4973.84
Posterior marginals for linear predictor and fitted values computed

Does this DIC have any information from the missing data?  In Win/OpenBUGS missing data models can often give negative DIC values, or DIC is not interpretable, so how is INLA doing this, and is the DIC interpretable in missing data models?
I would be most grateful for any advice

Corey

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inference under spde model with known variance and scale parameters
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] inference under spde model with known variance and scale parameters
messages.body_plain:
[Initial reply didn't go to the list. /FL]
Note: This reply deals only with the "spde with fixed parameters" bit,
and assumes general knowledge of how to do inference with inla.

On 7 November 2012 15:03, gg <gilles.b...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I would like to do inference with a formula along the line of
> myformula =(z ~ 1 + f(spatial, model=spde) + y)
> where the spatial and scale parameters for the random field are known and
> fixed to  some values.
>
> How would I do that?

Hi,

first you need to figure out what tau and kappa should be in the SPDE
model.  How that can be done depends on your definition of "range".
With the definitions used in the SPDE/GMRF paper,
  kappa = sqrt(8*\nu)/range,
where nu=alpha-dim/2, so nu=1 when alpha=2 and dim=2.
For alpha=2 and dim=2, the field variance is given by
  \sigma^2 = 1/( 4\pi \kappa^2 \tau^2)
so that
  \tau = 1/( 4\pi \kappa^2 \sigma^2)^0.5

Then, construct the spde model object like this:

  spde=inla.spde2.matern(mesh,B.tau=matrix(log(tau),1,1),B.kappa=matrix(log(kappa),1,1))

this gives an spde model with no parameters, and the given values for
tau and kappa, by specifying them as offsets (in log scale), and no
basis functions for which to apply any "theta".

/Finn

> Thx
>
> G.
>

--
Finn Lindgren

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inla.mesh.create having tough time to converge?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] inla.mesh.create having tough time to converge?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
you've stumbled on one of the hard-to-fix bugs in the meshing
software: It doesn't always detect when the input data generates a
non-unique Delaunay triangulation, which then sometimes leads to an
infinite loop where a single edge is flipped back and forth, between
two equally "good" triangulations.  This is what happens for your very
regularly placed data.  If you are on Linux (perhaps also Mac), you
can see what's happening by adding plot.delay=1 to the
inla.mesh.create command.

One solution is to make very small random perturbations to the input data.
In your case, it turns out that it is enough to shift the values by a
common amount, even something as simple as "+1".  At least on my
computer, the following works:

loc = as.matrix(read.table("s.txt"))  ## Read the data
mesh = inla.mesh.create(loc+1, ...) ## Shift input to avoid numerical
ambiguity problems in fmesher
mesh$loc = mesh$loc-1 ## Shift the output back again.

/Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] spatial temporal model
messages.body_plain:
On 30 November 2012 09:47, jones <jonesmu...@gmail.com> wrote:
> am getting this error but i cannot figure out what am doing wrong. can some
> one help

You are supplying two A-matrices (A.est and 1=identity) but only one
set of covariates.
This is a single list:  c(field.indices, list(Intercept=1))
If you don't have any other covariates in the model, you just need to
drop the second A-matrix.
If you have any observation-specific covariates, add them in a second
list, like this:

effects=
  list(c(field.indices, list(Intercept=1)),
        list(other.covariate=something) )

/Finn
